questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against reflexively targeting "five nines" for every service?
options: Five nines is mathematically impossible to measure with current monitoring tools
It hands engineering an error budget so small that shipping anything new becomes risky, for reliability gains most users may never notice
Customers are legally required to be told when a service exceeds four nines
Five nines only applies to database systems, never to web applications
questions.explain: An overly tight SLO consumes the error budget's purpose: it leaves almost no room to safely ship changes, for a reliability improvement that may not be worth what it costs to achieve.

questions.q: What should be the first real step when picking an SLO target for an existing service?
options: Copy the SLO that a competitor advertises publicly
Set the target to 99.999% by default and adjust downward only after a major outage
Pull real historical SLI data (e.g. 90 days of latency/availability) to see what the service is already delivering
Ask engineering to vote on a number in a single meeting with no data
questions.explain: Starting from a service's actual measured performance avoids inventing a target from thin air, and often reveals whether the service is already near a natural ceiling.

questions.q: Why might an e-commerce platform want separate SLOs for its browse and checkout journeys instead of one blended SLO for the whole platform?
options: Legal requirements mandate a different SLO for every page on a commercial website
Browse and checkout always run on physically separate servers
A blended SLO is always mathematically invalid and cannot be calculated

The two journeys carry very different stakes for a failure — a checkout failure costs revenue immediately, while a browse slowdown is barely noticed — so one shared number hides where effort should actually go
questions.explain: Different user journeys tolerate failure differently. Writing one SLO per journey that matters keeps the target meaningful instead of averaging away the distinction.

questions.q: In the illustrative negotiation this lesson describes, what does the business side contribute that engineering cannot generate on its own?
options: The exact on-call staffing schedule for the next quarter
The actual downstream cost and stakes of a specific kind of failure, such as what a checkout outage during a sale costs in lost revenue and support load
The source code for the retry logic needed to hit a tighter SLO
The historical latency and availability numbers from the monitoring system
questions.explain: Engineering brings the data on cost and effort to hit a target; the business brings the real-world stakes of a given kind of failure, which only that side can assess.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend reviewing an SLO on a recurring cadence instead of setting it once?
options: A chronically exhausted or comfortably unspent error budget is useful information that the original target may be unrealistic or too loose, and reviewing keeps the number honest as the service and business change
SLOs legally expire every 90 days and must be reauthorized
Cloud providers automatically reset all SLOs every quarter
Reviewing is only needed if the service has never had an incident
questions.explain: A service, its traffic, and business priorities change over time. A periodic review checks whether the error budget's actual behavior still matches what the SLO assumed, and adjusts if not.
